title: Your Children May Forget the Sermons. They Won’t Forget What Happened When You Got Angry.
paragraphs: Your Children May Forget the Sermons. They Won’t Forget What Happened When You Got Angry.

You can teach them Bible verses every night, take them to church every Sunday, and tell them about the love of God—but one frightening moment of uncontrolled anger can preach a sermon their heart remembers for years.
There are sermons your children may forget.
They may forget the preacher’s three points.
They may forget the Sunday school lesson about patience.
They may forget the memory verse you practiced with them in the car.
They may even forget some of those nights when you opened the Bible at the dinner table and tried, with all the sincerity you had, to teach them who God is.
But there are other moments children remember with terrifying clarity.
The sound of your footsteps coming down the hallway.
The change in your voice.
The slammed door.
The plate hitting the table harder than necessary.
The sentence you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
The look on your face when something small suddenly became something enormous.
And sometimes…
the silence afterward.
That terrible silence when everybody in the house knows something happened, but nobody knows whether it is safe to talk about it.
Years later, your child may not remember what started the argument.
But they may remember how small they felt standing in front of you.

That is why one quiet sentence in Colossians deserves the attention of every Christian father, every Christian mother, every grandparent, guardian, and every believer entrusted with the heart of a child.
Paul writes:
Hoi pateres, mē erethizete ta tekna hymōn, hina mē athymōsin.
A faithful rendering is:
“Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they may not become discouraged.”
The Greek matters.
Paul uses ἐρεθίζετε — erethizete.
It carries the idea of provoking, irritating, stirring up, exasperating.
Then comes the consequence Paul is concerned about:
ἀθυμῶσιν — athymōsin.
To become discouraged.
To become disheartened.
To lose heart.
Paul is not merely concerned about whether children obey.
He is concerned about what can happen inside them while adults are trying to make them obey.
Read that again.
Because some parents have won arguments while slowly losing access to their child’s heart.
Some have corrected behavior while crushing courage.
Some have demanded respect while behaving in ways for which they themselves desperately needed to repent.
Some have been so determined to establish authority that they forgot Christian authority is never permission for uncontrolled flesh.
And Scripture does not only speak to the child.
That matters.
Because it is easy to quote, “Children, obey your parents.”
It is considerably more uncomfortable when the Bible turns toward the parent.
But it does.
“Fathers…”
God sees you too.
Not merely the child who disobeyed.
Not merely the teenager who talked back.
Not merely the spilled drink, unfinished homework, broken rule, messy bedroom, forgotten chore, bad grade, disrespectful tone, scratched car, missed curfew, or embarrassing scene in public.
God sees what happens inside you when those things happen.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Something happens.
Your body tightens.
Your patience disappears.
Your voice changes.
You tell yourself you are “correcting” them.
But somewhere inside, correction has stopped being correction.
Now you are unloading.
Yesterday’s stress.
Money problems.
Exhaustion.
Pressure at work.
Conflict in your marriage.
Your own childhood wounds.
The disappointment you never processed.
The fear that you are failing as a parent.
The frustration that nobody seems to listen until you become loud.
And suddenly your child is standing in front of an emotional storm they did not create.
They may have done something wrong.
Absolutely.
Biblical parenting does not mean pretending disobedience does not matter. Scripture teaches correction, instruction, discipline, boundaries, obedience, and parental authority.
But biblical authority and uncontrolled anger are not the same thing.
The child may genuinely need correction.
The parent may simultaneously need repentance.
Those truths can exist in the same room.
That is one of the hardest lessons Christian parents ever learn.
Being right about what your child did does not automatically make you right about how you responded.
You can have the correct rule…
and the wrong spirit.
You can defend a biblical standard…
with an unbiblical temper.
You can demand an apology…
while owing one yourself.
You can tell your child to control their emotions while demonstrating that you cannot control yours.
And children notice contradictions adults imagine they cannot see.
They notice how Dad behaves when inconvenienced.
They notice how Mom speaks when exhausted.
They notice whether Christianity survives traffic.
Whether grace survives spilled milk.
Whether patience survives disrespect.
Whether humility survives being challenged.
Whether Jesus is still Lord when the house gets loud.
That may be where some of the deepest discipleship happens.
Not when everybody is dressed nicely for church.
When somebody spills something.
When somebody lies.
When somebody breaks the expensive thing.
When your teenager says the sentence that hits the nerve you thought was healed.
When you are tired.
When nobody is watching.
When you have every opportunity to explode.
Because your children are not merely listening to what you say about Jesus.
They are watching what Jesus is doing to you.
James gives Christians a brutally practical command: be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. The Greek says βραδὺς εἰς ὀργήν — bradys eis orgēn—slow toward anger.
Slow.
Not incapable of recognizing wrong.
Not passive toward sin.
Not afraid to exercise authority.
Slow to anger.
Why?
James continues by warning that human anger does not produce the righteousness God requires.
That sentence should stop us.
Because how many times have we used anger in an attempt to manufacture righteousness?
We become louder because we want immediate obedience.
We intimidate because patience feels inefficient.
We shame because shame gets a reaction.
We threaten because fear produces fast compliance.
And sometimes it works.
For the moment.
The child becomes quiet.
The teenager walks away.
The room freezes.
You “win.”
But Colossians asks a deeper question:
What is happening to their heart?
Hina mē athymōsin.
So they do not become discouraged.
So they do not lose heart.

This does not mean every raised voice permanently damages a child. It does not mean faithful parents never become angry, never fail, or never need to speak firmly. Scripture itself distinguishes anger from sin when it commands believers not to sin in their anger.
The issue is not perfection.
The issue is what rules the home when imperfection appears.
Pride?
Or repentance?
Fear?
Or grace?
Image management?
Or truth?
Because there is another sermon your children may remember for the rest of their lives.
It begins after you failed.
You walk back into the room.
Your child expects another lecture.
Instead, you sit down.
Maybe your voice shakes.
Maybe this feels humiliating because nobody ever apologized to you when you were a child.
Maybe your father believed admitting wrong would weaken his authority.
Maybe your mother never said the words you spent decades wishing you could hear.
But now the Gospel gives you another way.
You look into your child’s eyes and say:
“What you did was wrong, and we still need to deal with it. But the way I spoke to you was wrong too. I sinned in my anger. I should not have treated you that way. Please forgive me.”
Imagine what just happened.
You did not surrender your authority.
You demonstrated where your authority ultimately comes from.
You showed your child that Dad answers to Jesus.
Mom answers to Jesus.
Everybody in this house stands beneath the Word of God.
You showed them that Christianity is not a system where powerful people use Scripture to control weaker people.
It is a kingdom where sinners bow before a holy King.
Including parents.
Especially parents.
And suddenly your failure becomes a doorway into something beautiful.
Your child learns what repentance looks like before they can spell theology.
They learn that confession is not humiliation.
They learn that authority can admit wrong.
They learn that love does not disappear after conflict.
They learn that forgiveness is more than something Christians talk about.
They watch it happen three feet away.
This is where the Gospel enters the living room.
Because Christianity was never the announcement that good families finally learned how to behave perfectly.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners have a Savior.
Jesus Christ did not come for parents who never lose patience.
He came for sinners.
He came for the father ashamed of what he shouted last night.
He came for the mother crying in the bathroom because she became the kind of parent she swore she would never become.
He came for the adult child still carrying memories of a home where anger felt more powerful than affection.
He came for families carrying wounds nobody discusses at church.
He came for the guilty.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The wounded.
The ones who need forgiveness.
The ones who need to forgive.
The ones who do not know how.
And He did not come merely to make us feel better about what happened.
He came to redeem us.
At the cross, Jesus does not excuse sin.
He bears its judgment.
Grace does not say your anger did not matter.
Grace says your anger mattered so much that Christ had to die for sin—and His mercy is so great that repentant sinners can actually be forgiven and changed.
That is the difference between shame and conviction.
Shame whispers:
“Hide.”
Jesus calls:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“Pretend it never happened.”
Jesus says:
“Confess.”
Shame says:
“You ruined everything.”
The Gospel says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And maybe someone reading this needs that sentence desperately.
You cannot go backward.
You cannot become the parent you were ten years ago and unsay every word.
You cannot climb into your child’s memories and delete every frightening night.
You cannot erase the moment they saw you lose control.
But you can repent today.
You can ask forgiveness today.
You can seek reconciliation today.
You can get help today.
You can break patterns today.
You can stop defending what God is asking you to confess.
And if your children are grown?
Call them.
Not to explain yourself.
Not to tell them how difficult they were.
Not to remind them that you provided food and paid the bills.
Not to demand that they acknowledge everything you did right before you acknowledge what you did wrong.
Just tell the truth.

“I have been thinking about some things from when you were growing up. There were times my anger hurt you. I cannot change those moments, and I don't want to make excuses for them. I am sorry. If there are things you need to tell me, I want to listen.”
Then listen.
Really listen.
You may hear things differently than they remember them.
You may disagree with parts of their interpretation.
But reconciliation does not begin with winning the historical argument.
Sometimes it begins with enough humility to hear the pain.
And if you are the adult child reading this rather than the parent…
perhaps your hands are shaking a little.
Because you remember.
You remember the footsteps.
The shouting.
The unpredictable moods.
The words nobody should have said to a child.
Maybe you became excellent at reading faces because childhood taught you to detect danger before anyone spoke.
Maybe you became quiet.
Maybe funny.
Maybe invisible.
Maybe successful.
Maybe rebellious.
Maybe religious.
Anything that helped you survive emotionally.
And perhaps the most complicated part is that the person who frightened you also took you to church.
So somewhere along the way, authority, anger, Christianity, and God became tangled together in your heart.
Hear this carefully:
Your earthly parent is not the measure of your heavenly Father.
Jesus reveals God perfectly.
Look at Christ.
Look at the One who welcomed children.
Look at the One who touched people others avoided.
Look at the One who confronted hypocrisy yet showed astonishing tenderness to the broken.
Look at the Savior who knew every sinful thing about His people and still went willingly toward the cross.
If somebody used Christian authority badly, Jesus is not asking you to pretend it was good.
He is inviting you to discover what His authority actually looks like.
Holy.
True.
Strong.
Merciful.
Never sinful.
And if this article exposed something hidden in your own parenting, do not run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
Maybe tonight does not need another promise that you will “try harder.”
Maybe it needs confession.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Perhaps those are the three most important words you could say.
And perhaps your child needs to hear the next ones.
“Please forgive me too.”
There is no prize for pretending.
We are not building a community of perfect Christians.
We are gathering around a perfect Christ.
And if you know a father who loves Jesus but is exhausted…
If you know a mother quietly wondering whether she is failing…
send this to her.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
Because the next time anger rises, you may need to remember one Greek word:
athymōsin.
Discouraged.
Lose heart.
Before you raise your voice, remember the heart standing in front of you.
Before you unload your frustration, remember whose little soul has been entrusted to your care.
Before you demand repentance, remember that the cross has made repentance possible for you too.
We want this ministry to remain a place where Scripture is not merely posted—it is opened, wrestled with, lived, and brought into the rooms where people actually hurt.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church or other faithful Christian giving.
It does not.
The New Testament teaches generosity that comes from the heart rather than compulsion. Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully.
One share may put this message in front of the parent who was about to explode tonight.
One tag may reach the father who has never learned how to apologize.
One saved article may be reopened five minutes before somebody repeats the pattern that wounded them as a child.
One honest comment may make another believer realize they are not the only Christian struggling with anger.
One invitation to follow may lead someone toward Scripture who has been surviving on spiritual crumbs.
Never underestimate what God can do with something faithfully placed in another person's path.
Your children may forget many of your sermons.
But imagine what happens if one of their strongest memories becomes this:
“My parent sometimes failed. But when they did, they came back. They admitted it. They asked forgiveness. They kept running to Jesus. And over the years…I watched Christ change them.”
That is a sermon too.
Maybe one of the most powerful you will ever preach.
Because your children do not need you to convince them that you are flawless.
They need to see what a sinner looks like when grace becomes real.
Tonight, the loudest sermon in your house may never come from a Bible held in your hand.
It may come from the moment you lower your voice, bend your pride, walk back through the door, look your child in the eyes, and say:
“I was wrong. Jesus is still changing me. Will you forgive me?”
Some children will forget the night you lost your temper—but they may spend a lifetime remembering the night grace brought you back through the door.
